paras: The killing of Rafe Harvey was the shooting and beating of a Black man by police officers and citizens in Savannah, Georgia, early on November 15, 1903, after he had wounded two officers and a railroad engineer while resisting arrest. Patrolman Harmon Miller shot him twice, and officers and citizens clubbed him before he was taken prisoner. Harvey died in the jail hospital two weeks later, and the only coverage found, in the Savannah Morning News, told the story entirely from the police side.

The Savannah Morning News described Harvey, whose first name it printed as Raphael, Reaf and Rafe, as a man "well know in police circles" who had fought officers on several occasions. According to the paper, he had beaten Officer Mose Davis and escaped in Oglethorpe lane some months earlier, during a summer of burglaries for which he was under suspicion. Davis and Detective Murphy were searching for a man who had held up and robbed a Miss McLeod when Davis came upon Harvey in Perry lane.

Davis, in plain clothes, arrested Harvey on suspicion, but Harvey broke away; in Davis's statement Harvey simply pulled free and ran, while the later account says he first struck Davis under the eye. Davis fired one shot as Harvey fled into a house and barricaded it. When Davis, Patrolman Enoch Hartley and Seaboard Air Line engineer John Goolsby tried to enter with a borrowed bicycle lamp, Harvey knocked out the light and, in the dark, struck all three on the head with an iron bar and a flatiron. Hartley was beaten unconscious, and he and Goolsby were sent to the Savannah Hospital.

Harvey escaped over a back fence, and a squad of police led by Mounted Sergeant Wood searched the nearby lanes. Reports of how long the search took range from about twenty minutes to several hours. Patrolman Miller found Harvey in an outbuilding or stable in Liberty lane and, by the police account, fired twice when Harvey sprang at him. Officers and citizens then beat the wounded man with clubs and billies, leaving him with "a dozen wounds", and the paper reported that police had difficulty keeping the citizens who gathered from "finishing the negro."

Harvey was taken to the police station house and then to the hospital at the county jail, where his condition was considered dangerous. Police held the iron bar and flatiron as evidence, and the paper said he would face three charges of assault with intent to murder if he recovered. He died in the jail hospital on the night of November 28, and no report of an inquest or of any inquiry into the shooting or the beating was found. In January 1904 the superintendent of police included the case in his annual report, saying Harvey was shot "when about to attack Patrolman Miller."

All five items found ran in the Savannah Morning News, and each rests on police sources; the November 16 story was drawn from Davis's statement to the superintendent. Headlines called Harvey a "DESPERATE NEGRO" and a "NEGRO DESPERADO", and the text described him as "vicious", "burly" and "notorious." The paper said Miller "was forced to shoot" and reported the citizens' attempt to finish off the wounded prisoner, and its description of him as "insolent", without comment.
No report of the case was found in the Black press, and no account from Harvey or from any witness outside the police and the men he fought appears in the coverage.

The November 29 obituary dates the fight "Feb. 15", although the same article says it occurred two weeks earlier and the reports of November 15 and 16 place it that morning. The first report named the engineer as Frank Goolsby of the Central Railway, which the next day's paper corrected to John Goolsby of the Seaboard Air Line. Accounts also differ on where Miller's bullets struck, giving the arm and body in one report and the shoulder and abdomen in another.

accounts.label: Police account (Savannah Morning News)
accounts.gist: Harvey resisted arrest, wounded three men with an iron bar in a darkened house, escaped, and lunged at Patrolman Miller, who shot him in self-defense; officers and citizens then clubbed him to subdue him.

accounts.label: Officer Davis's statement
accounts.gist: Harvey pulled away from Davis at Perry lane and Montgomery street, Davis fired one shot as he ran, and Harvey barricaded himself in a house where the fight took place in the dark.

accounts.label: Police superintendent's annual report
accounts.gist: In November Harvey beat Davis, Hartley and Goolsby, was shot by Miller 'when about to attack' him in a Liberty lane stable, and died in the county jail from his wounds.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News called Harvey a 'desperate negro', 'notorious', 'vicious' and a 'negro desperado', said Miller 'was forced to shoot', and reported that citizens wanted to finish him off without criticism.
